Special histological stains for light microscopy:
1- Silver (Ag): stains Golgi apparatus, nerve cells and fibers with brown and
reticular fibers with black.
2- Neutral stain: e.g. Leishman's stain it is a mixture of acidic and basic stains.
Used to demonstrate blood cells.
3- Vital stain: Staining the living cells inside the living animal. It is used to stain
cells as they phagocytose the stain e.g. trypan blue and Indian ink.
4- Supravital stain: Staining living cells outside the living body, e.g. staining
reticulocytes (immature RBCs) with Brilliant cresyl blue.
5- Metachromatic stain: the stain gives a new color different from that of the
stain, e.g. Toluidine blue; when it stains basophil of blood or mast cell. It reacts
with the mucopolysaccharides in their granules giving a violet color.
6- Histochemical stains: Need the frozen technique.
To demonstrate enzymes or chemical components of the cells, e.g.:
a. Periodic Acid-Schiff reaction (PAS): stains glycogen with magenta red color.
b. Fat stains: e.g. Sudan III stains fat with orange color.
c. Enzymes: Include acid & alkaline phosphatases as enzymes of lysosome.
7- Orcein stain: it stains elastic fibers with brown color.
8- Immunohistochemical stains:
Using antibodies to demonstrate specific antigens (as the proteins of intermediate
filaments). Antibodies labeled with a dye to emit visible color.

Functions of cell membrane:
A. Endocytosis: Bulk movement of substance into the cell by forming vesicles;
spans.label: A. Endocytosis

spans.text: include three types:
1. Phagocytosis (cell eating):
• Pseudopodia extended from the cell to surround the particle e.g. a bacterium.
• The membranes of these extensions meet and fuse enclosing the bacterium in an
intracellular vacuole called phagosome.
• The phagosome then fuses with a lysosome for digestion of its contents.
• Example: WBCs engulfing bacteria.
2. Pinocytosis (cell drinking):
• Smaller invaginations of cell membrane form and surround extracellular fluid.
• Pinocytic vesicles then detach off inwardly from the cell membrane.
• The vesicle usually fuses with a lysosome for digestion of its contents.
• Example: pinocytosis of colloid in thyroid follicular cell.
3. Receptor mediated endocytosis:
• Receptors in the form of integral proteins in cell membrane bind to specific
substances and aggregate at the site of binding.
• They associate with other proteins on the cytoplasmic side called clathrin to form
a coated pit.
• The coated pit invaginates and pinches off, forming a coated vesicle containing
the specific substances and their receptors internally.
• Example: uptake of protein hormones as GH by the cell.

➢ 2ry lysosomes: lysosomes with variable contents, so appear by EM as different

Types of the 2ry lysosomes according to their content:
a. Heterolysosome: Formed by fusion of a primary (1ry) lysosome with a
phagosome to digest solid particles as bacteria or virus.
b. Multivesicular body: Formed by fusion of a 1ry lysosome with a pinocytic
vesicle to digest fluid particles.
c. Autolysosome: Formed by fusion of
a 1ry lysosome with autophagic
vesicles containing destroyed
endogenous substrate as mitochondria.
Fate of secondary lysosomes:
The digested material diffuses to the cytoplasm through lysosomal membrane while
undigested material is retained within vesicles called residual bodies.
The residual body may:
1- Discharge the undigested material by exocytosis (cytostool)
2- Accumulate over years in long lived cells as cardiac muscle and nerve cells as
lipofuscin granules (age pigments).
Functions of lysosomes:
1. Digest nutrients and phagocytosed bacteria and viruses.
2. Maintain cell health by removal of excess or non functional organelles.
3. Postmortem autolysis by digestion of cell after death due to lysosomal rupture.
4. Fertilization by helping the head of sperm to penetrate the ovum.
5. Activation of thyroid hormone by breaking bond between hormone & protein.

2) Cilia
Definition: Motile processes with microtubular
spans.label: Definition

I- Basal body:
A centriole is formed of 27 microtubules in 9 triplets,
embedded in cytoplasm.
II- Shaft (axoneme):
• Finger-like cytoplasmic projection from cell surface covered by plasmalemma.
• From each triplet, A & B microtubules grow as doublets pushing the cell
membrane in front of them.
• So, the shaft is formed of 9 peripheral doublets and 2 singlet microtubules in the
center are formed by polymerization (20 microtubules).
III- Rootlets:
Formed by growth of microtubule C in each triplet of basal body into the cytoplasm
(9 MT). They fix the basal body and shaft to cytoplasm.
Functions of cilia:
a. Repeated beating motion by bending of adjacent doublets → moving secretions or
particles in one direction as in respiratory & female genital tracts.
b. Cilia can modify & act as receptors as in rods & cones of retina.
3) Flagella
• They are motile projections from the cell, designed to move the cell itself.
• They have exactly the same structure as the axoneme of the cilium (nine
peripheral doublets and 2 central singlets), but extremely longer.
• In human, a flagellum forms tail of the sperm, which helps its movements.
Inability of the cilia to move results in bacterial infections on top of
accumulated secretions causing chronic respiratory infections.
Immotile flagella cause male infertility

This tissue is called epithelial tissue because it is mostly cover the outer
surfaces or line the surfaces of cavities all over the body.
General Characters of epithelial tissue:
• Consists of crowded cells with minimal intercellular space between cells.
• The upper surface of epithelium is free. The basal surface rests on a basement
membrane which may be clear or not clear.
• Blood vessels and lymph vessels cannot penetrate between epithelial cells but
nerves can, so epithelium is avascular. It receives nutrition by diffusion from the
underlying connective tissue.
• Has a high power of regeneration (renewal).
Origin of epithelial tissue:
• Ectodermal: e.g. skin.
• Mesodermal: e.g. serous membranes.
• Endodermal: e.g. Gastrointestinal tract (GIT).
Epithelial tissue is classified into:
• Surface Epithelium: either covers surfaces or lines cavities
• Glandular Epithelium: its cells modify to give secretion
• Neuro-epithelium: its cells modify to act as receptor.
• Myo-epithelium: its cells have a contractile function.
I- SURFACE EPITHELIUM
Surface epithelium is classified according to its number of layers into:-
A- Simple epithelium. B- Stratified epithelium.
A- SIMPLE EPITHELIUM
It is called simple as it is formed of one layer of cells. All cells are resting on a
basement membrane. It is divided according to shape of cells into:-
1- Simple squamous epithelium.
2- Simple cubical epithelium.
3- Simple columnar epithelium.
4- Simple columnar ciliated epithelium.
5- Pseudo-stratified columnar epithelium.
1- Simple Squamous Epithelium:
• It is formed of ONE layer of flat cells with flat nuclei
resting on basement membrane.
• Functions: It provides
a- A smooth surface which is important for easy passage of fluids and easy
movement of organs.
b- A thin membrane that helps exchange of gases.
• Sites:
a. Lines blood vessels & heart forming smooth surface→ is called endothelium.
b. Lines lung alveoli forming thin membrane for exchange of gases→ is called
pneumocytes.
c. Lines serous membranes e.g. pleura, pericardium & peritoneum, form smooth
surface for easy movement of organs → is called mesothelium.
d. Lines Bowman’s capsule of kidney (filtration of blood).
2- Simple Cubical Epithelium:
• Formed of ONE layer of cube-shaped cells with central rounded nuclei.
• Functions: Secretion and reabsorption.
• Sites:
1- Secretory acini of glands. E.g. follicles
of thyroid gland.
2- Convoluted tubules of kidney.
3- Simple Columnar Epithelium:
• Formed of ONE layer of tall columnar cells
with basal oval nuclei
• Functions: Secretion and absorption.
• Sites:
Lines digestive tract e.g. stomach and small
& large intestine.
4- Simple Columnar Ciliated Epithelium:
• Formed of ONE layer of tall columnar cells with
basal oval nuclei; the cells are provided with cilia
• Functions: Cilia can transport fluid or particle
over the epithelial surface in one direction.
• Sites:
1- Lower respiratory tract (lung bronchioles),
to move secretions upwards.
2- Female genital system: uterus & fallopian tube to move the ovum.

• It is actually a type of simple epithelium because it is formed of one cell layer and
all cells rest on the basement membrane.
• Some of its columnar cells cannot reach the surface.
• The cells are very crowded so nuclei are present at more than one level; this gives
the epithelium a false appearance of being stratified.

II- GLANDULAR EPITHELIUM
❖ Definition:
A type of epithelium which modifies to act as a gland & produce secretion.
❖ According to the presence or absence of duct, the
glands are classified into:
• Exocrine gland:
Formed of secretory cells (secretory portion) which forms the secretion and ducts
(excretory portion) that carries the secretion to outside the gland.
• Endocrine gland (ductless gland):
Formed of groups of secretory cells and blood capillaries. But no ducts, their
secretion (hormones) is carried by blood to different parts of the body.
• Mixed gland:
Formed of two parts; exocrine part which has duct system and endocrine part with
no duct system.
❖ Classification of exocrine glands:
1- According to the number of cells forming the gland:
a) Unicellular gland: Formed of one cell.
b) Multicellular glands: Formed of more than one cell.
2- According to type (Nature) of secretion:
Watery secretion, serous secretion (watery secretion with enzymes) and
Mucus secretion
3- According to mode (mechanism) of secretion:
a) Merocrine secretion: The most common mechanism. Secretion is
discharged outside the cell by exocytosis so no changes occur in the
secretory cell.
b) Apocrine secretion: The secretion is released and come out with the apex
of the cell.
c) Holocrine secretion: The secretion accumulates in the cell, later on the
swollen cell ruptures and the whole cell is lost with the secretion.
4- According to branching of the duct:
a) Simple gland: The gland has a single non-branching duct with non-
branching secretory part.
When the secretory portion only is branched, the gland is called simple
branched.
b) Compound gland: The gland has a branching duct like a tree and
consequently, each duct branch has a secretory part.
5- According to shape of secretory part:
a) Tubular: Secretory unit is in the form of a tube.
b) Alveolar (Acinar): Secretory unit is rounded.
c) Tubuloalveolar: Secretory part is flask shape.

II- LATERAL SPECIALIZATIONS (Cell Junctions)
Lateral membrane of epithelial cells are linked together mainly via adhesive
transmembrane protein molecules. Different junctions are recognized:
1- Tight or occluding junction (Zonula Occludens):
• Two adjacent cell membranes fuse at certain points
via transmembrane protein molecules on each cell.
• It completely encircles the apex of the cell like a belt.
• Function: Restrict passage of substances between
adjacent cells.
2- Adherens Junction (Zonula Adherens):
• Two adjacent cell membranes are separated by wide intercellular space.
• In intercellular space, extracellular parts of transmembrane protein molecules on
two adjacent cell membranes are connected by the help of Ca ++ ions.
• At cytoplasmic side, condensed protein molecules bind transmembrane protein
molecules to actin filaments (cytoskeleton).
• Adherens Junction encircles the cell like a belt (so called zonula).
• Function: provide lateral adhesion between the epithelial cells.
3- Macula Adherens (Desmosomes):
• Wide intercellular space shows Ca++
dependent interconnection between
extracellular portions of transmembrane
protein molecules.
• The cytoplasmic side is thickened and called
attachment plaque that is composed of
several protein types which are capable of
anchoring the intermediate filaments.
• Macula adherens does not encircle the cell
but is scattered as circular spots (so called
macula).
• Present between epithelial cells especially in
stratified squamous epithelium.
• Functions: The strongest type of junctions
that provide firm adhesions among the cells to
support the surfaces subjected to friction.
Junctional Complex:
It usually includes three types of junctions (zonula occludens, zonula adherens and
desmosomes) are present between adjacent cells e.g. simple columnar cells lining the
small intestine.
4- Gap junction (Nexus) communicating junction:
• Two adjacent cell membranes are separated by a narrow gap but connected by
narrow channels that bridge the intercellular space.
• Each channel is formed of 6 symmetrical molecules of transmembrane protein.
• Functions:
1- Exchange of ions and small molecules between adjacent epithelial cells.
2- Passage of impulses between muscle cells.
III- BASAL SPECIALIZATIONS
1- Hemidesmosomes:
• Take the shape of half a desmosome at basal
part of basal cells.
• Function: Fix epithelium to underlying basement
membrane and connective tissue.
2- Basement membrane:
It is an amorphous dense layer located next to basal surface of epithelial cells.

Morphology of the mature gametes:
I-Sperm (male gamete): (Figure 1.1)
spans.label: I-Sperm (male gamete)

spans.text: Human sperm is 55 microns long and consists of the following parts:
It is 4 microns long and contains:
 Condensed nucleus that carries hereditary material of the father (22 autosomes
& X or Y chromosome).
 Acrosomal cap is a sac that contains hyaluronidase and acrosin enzymes and
surrounds most of the nucleus.
 It contains minimal cytoplasm.
 It is surrounded by cell membrane.
Neck: It is the narrow part between the head and the middle piece of the sperm.
spans.label: Neck

spans.text: Middle piece: It is 6 microns long and is composed of mitochondrial sheath around the
spans.label: Middle piece

spans.text: proximal part of axial filament. It is the source of energy for sperm motility.
Tail: It is 45 microns long and is composed of an axial filament that is surrounded by
spans.label: Tail

spans.text: minimal cytoplasm and cell membrane. The tail directs the movement of the sperms
towards the ovum during fertilization.
II-Ovum: (Figure 1.2)
spans.label: II-Ovum

spans.text: The diameter of the mature ovum is about 120 microns.
It consists of:
Secondary oocyte: It carries a nucleus that has the hereditary material of the mother
spans.label: Secondary oocyte

spans.text: (22 autosomes & X- chromosome). It contains a large cytoplasm that is the initial
source of nutrition of the zygote. It is surrounded by three coverings (from inner to
 Cell membrane.
 Zona pellucida: It is a glycoprotein coat that surrounds the cell membrane. It
carries sperm receptors.
(Anatomy) Gametes 2
 Corona radiata: It is the outer cover that is formed of follicular cells that are
adherent to each other by hyaluronic acid.
(Anatomy) First Week of Development 3
Chapter 2
By the end of this chapter, the student should be able to:
 Know the term fertilization.
 Understand the steps of fertilization.
 Figure out the expected results of fertilization.
 Describe the cleavage and migration of developing embryo and formation of the
blastocyst.
First Week of Development
Fertilization
It is the process by which sperm and ovum unite to form a zygote.
Site of fertilization: (Figure 2.1) Fertilization occurs in the ampullary part of the
spans.label: Site of fertilization

spans.text: uterine tube (lateral third).
Steps of fertilization: (Figure 2.2)
spans.label: Steps of fertilization

spans.text: A-Capacitation of sperms
It is the process of removal of glycoprotein coat that covers the acrosomal region of the
sperms in the female genital system and it takes about 7 hours to be completed.
B-Phase I (Dispersion of corona radiata cells)
Only 300 – 500 sperms out of 200 – 300 million sperms / ejaculate reach the ovum and
start dispersing corona radiata cells by the release of hyaluronidase enzyme. This will
open passages between corona radiata cells.
C-Phase II (Penetration of zona pellucida)
After passing through the corona radiata, sperms are drawn to the zona pellucida by
specific receptors. Sperm's head then binds to the zona, triggering the release of
enzymes like acrosin and trypsin-like material from its acrosomal cap. These enzymes
dissolve a path through the zona, allowing the fertilizing sperm, propelled by tail
(Anatomy) First Week of Development 4
movements, to pass through. Then the head of the fertilizing sperm comes in contact to
cell membrane of the secondary oocyte. This phase is known as acrosomal reaction.
D-Phase III (Opening of the cell membrane of the oocyte):
At this phase both cell membranes of the head of the fertilizing sperm and oocyte fuse
together. Then the fused membranes open to allow the passage of contents of
fertilizing sperm (nucleus, mitochondrial sheath and axial filament) to the cytoplasm of
the oocyte.
Event that occurs during the passage of contents of fertilizing sperm to
cytoplasm of ovum
Cortical and zona reaction: (Figure 2.3)
spans.label: Cortical and zona reaction

spans.text: It is a process that prevents polyspermy through the release of lysosomal enzymes
from cortical granules that lie inner to the cell membrane of the oocyte. These enzymes
prevent entrance of other sperms through the following mechanisms:
 Changing the structure of sperm receptors in the zona pellucida to
stop attraction of more sperms.
 Making the cell membrane and zona pellucida of the fertilized oocyte,
impenetrable to other sperms than the fertilizing one.
Event that occurs after the passage of contents of fertilizing sperm to cytoplasm
a) The nucleus of the secondary oocyte completes the second meiotic
division to form nucleus of ootid and second polar body. Then maturation of the
nucleus will form female pronucleus.
b) Sperm nucleus becomes larger to be male pronucleus.
c) Nuclear membranes of both male and female pronuclei, fuse together
to form the nucleus of the zygote.
Results of fertilization:
1) Formation of the zygote.
2) Determination of the sex of the zygote; either male (XY) or female
(XX) and this is according to the type of fertilizing sperm.
3) Restoration of diploid number of chromosomes (46 chromosomes), as
nuclei of each sperm or ovum contains haploid number of chromosomes (23
chromosomes).
4) Start of cleavage and migration of the zygote from fertilization site to
implantation in the uterine cavity.
(Anatomy) First Week of Development 5
Cleavage and Migration (Figure 2.4)
Zygote divides mitotically within the zona pellucida coat, giving rise to smaller
blastomeres (46 chromosomes).
 On the first day, 2 blastomeres are formed.
 On the second day, 4 blastomeres are formed.
 On the third day, 8 blastomeres are formed. This is followed by the
formation of 16 blastomeres (morula), then 32 cells followed by 64 cells.
(Anatomy) First Week of Development 6
During cleavage, the embryo migrates inside the uterine tube to reach the uterine
cavity on the 4th day by the following mechanisms:
 Muscular peristalsis of the uterine tube.
 Moving cilia push the developing embryo towards the uterine cavity.
 Mucus secretion from the uterine tube facilitates migration and
provides nutrition to the developing embryo.
Blastocyst:
Formation of blastocyst: (Figure 2.4)
spans.label: Formation of blastocyst

spans.text: Morula reaches the uterine cavity on the 4th gestational day. On the end of the 5th day,
zona pellucida starts to degenerate. Uterine fluid passes through the degenerated zona
to form multiple spaces between cells of the morula. Gradually, those spaces fuse to
form a single cavity called blastocele. This embryonic stage is called blastocyst that
completes its development at the end of the 6th day.
Structure of the blastocyst: (Figure 2.5)
spans.label: Structure of the blastocyst

spans.text: It has the following features:
 Outer cell mass (trophoblast): It is the wall of the blastocyst that is formed of a
single cell layer.
 Inner cell mass (embryoblast): It is a mass of cells that lies inner to one side of
the trophoblast cells.
 Blastocele: It is the cavity of the blastocyst.
 Embryonic pole: It is the part of the trophoblast that lies outer to embryoblast.
 Abembryonic pole: It is the part of the trophoblast that lies on the opposite side
of the embryonic pole.
(Anatomy) Second Week of Development 7
Chapter 3
By the end of this chapter, the student should be able to:
 Define the term implantation and describe its mechanism.
 Oriented about the abnormal sites of implantation.
 Recognize decidua and understand its different parts.
 Know the steps of transformation of blastocyst to the chorionic vesicle.
Second Week of Development
Implantation
It is the process by which the blastocyst becomes embedded in the superficial layers of
endometrium.
Time: It begins at the 7th gestational day to be completed at the 11th gestational day.
spans.label: Time

spans.text: Site: In the endometrium of the upper part of the posterior wall of the uterus just below
spans.label: Site

spans.text: the fundus. Less frequent embryos may be implanted in the upper part of the anterior
wall of the uterus.
Features of endometrium of implantation: (Figure 3.1)
spans.label: Features of endometrium of implantation

spans.text: At the beginning of implantation, the endometrium is at secretory phase of menstrual
cycle. This phase is characterized by the increase of the following; thickness of
endometrium, number and size of endometrial cells, spiral glands that are filled with
secretion and spiral arteries with increased arterio-venous anastomosis.
(Anatomy) Second Week of Development 8
Mechanism of implantation (Figure 3.2)
• It starts with the adhesion of the blastocyst by its embryonic pole to
the endometrium at the implantation site.
• Trophoblast cells at the embryonic pole proliferate to form a new layer
of cells that have no cell membrane. This layer lies outer to trophoblast, starting
at the embryonic pole and increased in size with the progress of implantation, it
is called syncytiotrophoblast.
• Syncytiotrophoblast layer forms proteolytic enzyme that erodes the
endometrium at the site of implantation to form implantation cavity. Blastocyst
enters to this cavity to be completely embedded inside the endometrium on the
9th day. The penetrated site of endometrial epithelium becomes blocked by fibrin
• Two days later, on the 11th gestational day, the endometrial epithelium
proliferate to cover the fibrin clot.
Changes of the blastocyst during implantation
 Trophoblast layer differentiates into an outer syncytiotrophoblast layer
and an inner trophoblast layer. This change starts at the embryonic pole and
extends to cover the whole blastocyst with the progress of implantation process.
 Formation of amniotic cavity (at 8th day) and yolk sac (at the 9th day).
 Formation of bilaminar embryonic disc from the embryoblast.
(Anatomy) Second Week of Development 9
Abnormal sites of implantation: (Figures 3.3 & 3.4)
spans.label: Abnormal sites of implantation

spans.text: A-Intrauterine implantation
I- Placenta previa: It is the implantation in the lower segment of uterine cavity, where
spans.label: I- Placenta previa

spans.text: placenta is related to the internal os. (upper opening of cervical canal).
1. Complete (total) placenta: It covers the internal os completely.
2. Partial placenta: It covers the internal os partially.
3. Marginal: Lower edge of placenta lies at the margin of internal os.
II-Low lying placenta: It is the implantation in the lower segment of uterine cavity, where
spans.label: II-Low lying placenta

spans.text: the lower edge of placenta lies within two cm. away from the margin of internal os.
B-Ectopic pregnancy:
Tubal: It is due to implantation inside the uterine tube at ampulla, isthmus or intramural
spans.label: Tubal

spans.text: part. In this condition, rupture of the tube with internal hemorrhage is expected
maximally at the age of the 8th week of pregnancy.
Ovarian: Implantation on the surface of the ovary.
spans.label: Ovarian

spans.text: Omental: Implantation on the surface of the peritoneum.
spans.label: Omental

spans.text: (Anatomy) Second Week of Development 10
Decidua (Figure 3.5)
It is the endometrium after implantation.
Features of decidua:
Decidua shows increased thickness due to:
 Increased number and size of endometrial cells.
 Glands become spiral and dilated with increased secretion.
 Arteries become spiral and show arterio-venous anastomosis.
Parts of decidua:
1. Decidua basalis: It is the part of decidua between implanted embryo
and myometrium of uterus.
2. Decidua capsularis: It is the part of decidua that covers the embryo,
separating it from the uterine cavity.
3. Decidua parietalis: It is the part of decidua that lines the rest of the
uterine cavity.
Fate of decidua:
1. Decidua basalis (decidual plate): It persists to form the maternal part
of placenta.
2. Deciduae capsularis and parietalis: They fuse together with
obliteration of uterine cavity. These fused deciduae are expelled after delivery of
the baby.
Daily events during the second gestational week
Seventh gestational day: (Figure 3.6)
spans.label: Seventh gestational day

spans.text: • Blastocyst begins implantation.
• Trophoblast layer differentiates into inner cytotrophoblast and outer
syncytiotrophoblast, starting at the embryonic pole and extends to cover the
whole blastocyst with the progress of implantation. Syncytiotrophoblast cells
produce proteolytic enzyme that erodes the endometrium to form an
implantation cavity.
(Anatomy) Second Week of Development 11
Eighth gestational day: (Figure 3.7)
spans.label: Eighth gestational day

spans.text: • Blastocyst is partially embedded in the endometrium.
• Increased area of differentiated trophoblast layer into outer
syncytiotrophoblast and inner cytotrophoblast.
• Formation of hypoblast layer from cells of embryoblast that face the
blastocele, as those cells become cuboidal in shape.
• Formation of amniotic cavity within the rest of inner cell mass cells.
The cavity separates cells of the embryoblast into:
 Amnioblast: It is the layer of cells that lie in contact with
cytotrophoblast. It is the first source of amniotic fluid. It forms the roof of
the amniotic cavity.
 Epiblast: It is the layer of tall columnar cells that lie in contact with
hypoblast. It forms the floor of the amniotic cavity. Epiblast with hypoblast
forms the bilaminar embryonic disc.
(Anatomy) Second Week of Development 12
Ninth and tenth gestational days: (Figure 3.8)
spans.label: Ninth and tenth gestational days

spans.text: • Blastocyst is completely embedded in the endometrium.
• The penetrated endometrial epithelium is closed by fibrin clot.
• Formation of primary yolk sac: Blastocele is transformed into primary yolk sac after
formation of the Heuser’s membrane that is composed of flat cells and derived from
the hypoblast.
• Almost the whole wall of the blastocyst is differentiated into outer
syncytiotrophoblast and inner cytotrophoblast.
• Formation of lacunar spaces: They are empty spaces that are formed in the
syncytiotrophoblast layer (lacunar stage).
Eleventh and twelfth gestational days: (figure 3.9)
spans.label: Eleventh and twelfth gestational days

spans.text: • Endometrial epithelium overgrows and covers the fibrin clot to
complete implantation.
• Lacunar spaces become filled with maternal blood to form utero-
placental circulation.
• Formation of extra-embryonic mesoderm cells that are derived from
the wall of yolk sac. This mesodermal layer is formed between cytotrophoblast
(external) and embryonic disc with amniotic and yolk sac cavities (internal).
• Multiple large spaces appear in loose cells of the extra-embryonic
mesoderm.
(Anatomy) Second Week of Development 13
Thirteenth gestational day: (Figure 3.10)
spans.label: Thirteenth gestational day

spans.text: • Formation of chorionic vesicle: Spaces of extra-embryonic coelom communicate
to form a single cavity known as chorionic cavity (extra-embryonic coelom). Cells
of the extra-embryonic mesoderm are distributed into two layers:
1. Somatic (somatopleuric) mesoderm lines the cytotrophoblast and covers the
amniotic cavity.
2. Splanchnic (splanchopleuric) mesoderm covers the secondary yolk sac.
• Formation of the chorion: It is the wall of chorionic vesicle that is formed of 3
layers from inside to outside: somatic mesoderm, cytotrophoblast and
syncytiotrophoblast.
• Connecting stalk is the part of the extraembryonic mesoderm that connects
chorion with caudal end of the embryonic disc.
• Formation of new endodermal cells from hypoblast that migrate to form new
lining to the primary yolk sac, transforming it into secondary yolk sac. Pinching
off a large part of the secondary yolk sac with marked reduction of its size.
• Formation of a diverticulum from the caudal wall of secondary yolk sac that
extends inside the connecting stalk and is called allantois (Figure 3.11).
• Start formation of primary chorionic villi from chorion.
(Anatomy) Second Week of Development 14
(Anatomy) Third Week of Development 15
Chapter 4
By the end of this chapter, the student should be able to:
 Trace the changes that occur in the embryo during the 3 rd. week of pregnancy.
 Describe the development of the chorionic villi at different stages (primary,
secondary and tertiary).
 Cite the different parts of the 3ary villus and point to the function of each.
 Recognize the different parts of the chorionic villi and indicate the fate of each.
 Define and describe gastrulation.
 Describe the different stages of formation of the notochord, discuss its important
functions and indicate its fate.
 Review the site and differentiation of the intraembryonic mesoderm.
Third Week of Development
The most characteristic events that occur during the third gestational week are the
formation of chorionic villi and gastrulation of the embryonic disc.
Chorionic villi:
Time of formation:
They start formation at the end of the second week and complete at the end of the third
Primary villi: (Figure 4.1) Each villous is composed of a core of cytotrophoblast with a
spans.label: Primary villi

spans.text: cover of syncytiotrophoblast. They start formation at the end of the second week and
complete formation at the beginning of the third week. They are separated from each
other by lacunar spaces.
Secondary villi: (Figure 4.1) At the middle of third week, primary villi are transformed
spans.label: Secondary villi

spans.text: to secondary villi after incorporation of somatic mesoderm inside the core of the villus.
Each villus is composed of somatic mesoderm core that is surrounded by
cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast layers. They are separated from each other by
intervillous spaces.
(Anatomy) Third Week of Development 16
Tertiary chorionic villi (Figures 4.2 & 3)
By the end of the third week of development, secondary villi mature into tertiary
chorionic villi. This transformation occurs as fetal blood vessels develop within the
mesodermal core of the villi. Tertiary villi are separated from each other by intervillous
spaces. Each individual villus is structured from the inside out as follows:
 Somatic mesoderm core containing fetal blood vessels
 Cytotrophoblast layer
 Syncytiotrophoblast layer
Additionally, a cytotrophoblastic shell forms around the tertiary villi and intervillous
spaces. This shell originates from the cytotrophoblastic layer of the tertiary villi.
Parts of tertiary villi:
a) Stem (anchoring) villous: It is middle part of the villous that extends between
chorion and decidua basalis.
b) Free (floating or absorbing) villi: They are side branches from the stem part that
float in maternal blood in the intervillous spaces. They are the parts of tertiary
villi at which exchange of nutrient and gases between maternal and fetal blood
Parts of the chorion: (Figure 4.3)
spans.label: Parts of the chorion

spans.text: Chorion frondosum (chorionic plate): It is the part of the chorion that carry will
spans.label: Chorion frondosum (chorionic plate)

spans.text: developed tertiary villi that is in contact with the decidua basalis (decidual plate).
Chorion leave: It is the smooth remaining part of the chorion that carries degenerated
spans.label: Chorion leave

spans.text: tertiary villi and is covered with decidua capsularis.
Fate of the chorion:
Chorion frondosum (chorionic plate): It persists as the fetal part of placenta.
spans.label: Chorion frondosum (chorionic plate)

spans.text: Chorion leave: It fuses with deciduae capsularis and parietalis and degenerates.
spans.label: Chorion leave

spans.text: (Anatomy) Third Week of Development 17
Gastrulation (Figure 4.4)
It is the transformation of bilaminar embryonic disc into trilaminar disc. This process
begins by formation of primitive streak and node in the epiblast layer.
Primitive streak:
It is a median narrow groove with bulging sides that are formed in the midline of the
caudal part of the epiblast layer. It is developed due to proliferation and migration of
epiblast cells towards the primitive groove through which they pass.
Primitive node:
It is a rounded bulge at the cranial end of primitive streak with a middle primitive pit.
Invagination:
Epiblast cells pass through the primitive groove to form:
 Endodermal layer replaces the hypoblast.
 Intra-embryonic mesoderm which forms a middle layer in the embryonic disc.
 Notochord in the median region of the embryonic disc.
 The rest of epiblast layer is called ectoderm and its junction with amnion is
known as amnio-ectodermal junction.
N.B. The three layers of the embryonic disc are derived from the epiblast layer.
Bucco-pharyngeal (prochordal) membrane:
It is a rounded area of fusion between ectoderm and endoderm at the cranial part of
embryonic disc.
Cloacal membrane:
It is a rounded area of fusion between ectoderm and endoderm at the caudal part of
embryonic disc.
N.B. During the third gestational week, embryonic disc changes its shape from oval to
pear shape with broader cranial part. (Figure 4.5)
(Anatomy) Third Week of Development 18
Notochord
It is the temporary primitive axial skeleton of the embryonic disc.
Steps of development:
1-Prenotochordal process: (Figure 4.6)
It is formed by invagination of solid cord of epiblast cells that are derived from the
primitive pit. It extends cranially in midline between ectoderm and endoderm till it
reaches the bucco-pharyngeal membrane.
(Anatomy) Third Week of Development 19
2-Notochordal canal: (Figure 4.7)
Primitive pit cavity extends into the prenotochordal process transforming it into
notochordal canal.
• Roof that lie in contact with ectoderm.
• Floor that is fused with endoderm in the midline.
• Cavity that is continuous with amniotic cavity.
3-Neurenteric canal and notochordal plate: (Figure 4.8)
It is the temporary communication between amniotic cavity and yolk sac. It is
developed due to degeneration of the floor of notochordal canal together with the fused
median region of endoderm. The persistent roof and sides of the notochordal canal is
called the notochordal plate. The sides of the plate are fused with the remaining
endoderm.
(Anatomy) Third Week of Development 20
4-Definitive notochord: (Figure 4.9)
Folding of the notochordal plate upon itself leads to the following:
• Formation of definitive solid notochord with no cavity.
• Approximation and fusion of endoderm on both sides of the developing
notochord so amniotic cavity and yolk sac regain their separation from each
Importance of notochord
 It is the temporary and primitive axial skeleton of the embryonic disc.
 During folding of the embryonic disc, its firmness limits head fold.
 Formation of vertebral column around the notochord.
Fate of notochord (Figure 4.10)
Most of notochord degenerates except the part within the intervertebral disc as it
persists to form nucleus pulposus.
(Anatomy) Third Week of Development 21
Intra-embryonic Mesoderm (Figure 4.11)
It is the middle layer between ectoderm and endoderm. It is derived from the epiblast
cells that pass through primitive streak and node during third gestational week. Intra-
embryonic mesoderm is not present in the following regions of the embryonic disc:
 At bucco-pharyngeal and cloacal membranes, due to fusion between ectoderm
and endoderm.
 Median region between primitive node and bucco-pharyngeal membrane, as
these areas are occupied by notochord and neural tube.
(Anatomy) Embryonic Period 22
CHAPTER 5
By the end of this chapter, the student should be able to:
 Determine the embryonic period and its significance.
 List the different structures and organs derived from each of the three germ
layers: ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm.
Embryonic Period
It is the period of organogenesis.
Time: It occurs from the 4th to 8th gestational weeks.
spans.label: Time

spans.text: Derivatives of ectoderm:
- Central nervous system.
- Derivatives of neural crest.
- Otic and lens placodes that form internal ear and lens of the eye respectively.
- Peripheral nerves, sensory epithelium of ear, nose, eye.
- Epidermis of the skin.
- Pituitary gland.
- Beginning and end of digestive tract.
Derivatives of endoderm:
1. Mucus lining epithelium of:
• Digestive system except its beginning and end.
• Respiratory tract.
• Most of urinary bladder and urethra.
• Tympanic cavity and Eustachian tube.
2. Glandular epithelium:
• Parenchyma of liver, pancreas, thyroid, thymus, tonsils (palatine &
nasopharyngeal) and parathyroid glands.
Intra-embryonic Mesoderm
It is the middle layer of the trilaminar embryonic disc.
Differentiation of intra-embryonic disc: (Figure 5.1)
spans.label: Differentiation of intra-embryonic disc

spans.text: On the 17th gestational day, it is divided into three parts:
I-Paraxial mesoderm:
It is the part of the intra-embryonic mesoderm that is present on both sides of the
notochord and neural tube. It is derived from epiblast cells that pass through the cranial
part of primitive streak.
II-Intermediate mesoderm:
It is the part of the intra-embryonic mesoderm that is present between paraxial and
lateral plate mesoderm. It is derived from epiblast cells that pass through the middle
part of primitive streak.
III-Lateral plate mesoderm:
It is the part of the intra-embryonic mesoderm that is lateral to intermediate mesoderm.
It is derived from epiblast cells that pass through the caudal part of primitive streak.
(Anatomy) Embryonic Period 23
1-Paraxial mesoderm (Figures 5.2 & 3)
It is part of the intra-embryonic mesoderm on both sides of the notochord and the
neural tube.
Segmentation:
Paraxial mesoderm divides transversely into segments known as somites.
Segmentation begins at the occipital region and extends caudally till coccygeal region.
Somitomeres are smaller segments that are present cephalic to the first occipital
Somites:
They are segmented masses of paraxial mesoderm.
Time of segmentation:
First pair of occipital somites are separated on the 20th gestational day. Then three
pairs of somites are separated each day till the 30th gestational day. Somite period is
from day 21 till day 30 as segmentation is regular. Then segmentation continues at a
slower and irregular rate till the 35th or 40th day.
Number of somites by day 40:
They are 42 – 44 pairs of somites.
Regional classification (from cranial to caudal):
Somites are regionally classified into 4 occipital pairs, 8 cervical pairs, 12 thoracic pairs,
5 lumbar pairs, 5 sacral pairs and 8 – 10 coccygeal pairs.
Determination of the age of the embryo (at somite period):
Age in days = Number of somites – 1
Differentiation
Each somite is divided obliquely into:
A-Sclerotome:
It is the ventromedial part of the somites. Cells of sclerotome migrate medially to
surrounds notochord and neural tube forming vertebrae and intervertebral discs.
(Anatomy) Embryonic Period 24
B-Dermomyotome:
It is the dorsolateral part of the somite that is further subdivided into:
1. Dermatome: It forms the dermis of the skin.
2. Myotome: It forms the skeletal muscles of the body.
Dermomyotome is divided into:
a) The dorsal part that forms skeletal muscle and dermis of the skin on the back of
vertebral column.
b) Ventral part that forms skeletal muscles and dermis of the skin of the rest of the
N.B. Spinal nerve divides into dorsal and ventral primary rami to supply the divided
dermomyotome.
2-Intermediate mesoderm (Figure 5.1)
It is the part of intra-embryonic mesoderm that lies between paraxial and lateral plate
mesoderm. It forms the urogenital system.
3-Lateral plate mesoderm (Figures 5.4 & 5)
It is the part of intra-embryonic mesoderm that lies lateral to intermediate mesoderm. It
is continuous with the opposite side mainly, cranial to bucco-pharyngeal membrane. It
is continuous with extra-embryonic mesoderm at the margin of the embryonic disc. Its
(Anatomy) Embryonic Period 25
cranial part is the septum transversum that forms the central tendon of diaphragm. The
part of the lateral plate mesoderm that lies between the serous pericardium and
endoderm is the cardiogenic area.
Intra-embryonic coelom
It is a horse-shoe cavity that is formed inside the lateral plate mesoderm. Its caudal
ends communicate with extra-embryonic coelom. It forms the serous sacs of the body
(serous pericardium, pleura and peritoneal canals).
The coelom divides the cells of lateral plate mesoderm into:
1. Somatopleuric (somatic) mesoderm that lies in contact with ectoderm. It forms
the lining connective tissue of the wall of the trunk and parietal layers of serous
sacs of the body.
2. Splanchopleuric (splanchnic) mesoderm that lies in contact with endoderm. It
forms connective tissue and smooth muscles of the gut, respiratory tract and
cardiac muscle. It also forms visceral layer of serous sacs of the body.
(Anatomy) Embryonic Period 26
Folding of the Embryonic Disc
It is the process by which the embryonic disc is folded upon itself.
Time of folding:
It begins at the end of the third week and is completed at the end of the fourth week.
Causes of folding:
A. Expansion of the amniotic cavity leads to longitudinal and transverse folding.
B. Growth of neural tube and somites lead to an increase of the longitudinal length
with subsequent cephalo-caudal folding.
Types of folding:
I-Cephalo-caudal (longitudinal) folding: It leads to formation of:
spans.label: I-Cephalo-caudal (longitudinal) folding

spans.text: 1. Head fold: It is the folding of the cranial part of the embryonic disc.
2. Tail fold: It is the folding of the caudal part of the embryonic disc.
II-Transverse (lateral) folding: It leads to formation of:
spans.label: II-Transverse (lateral) folding

spans.text: 1. Right lateral fold: It is folding of the right margin of the embryonic disc.
2. Left lateral fold: It is the folding of the left margin of the embryonic disc.
Limitations of head and tail folds
Head fold is limited by the relatively firm notochord while the tail fold is limited by the
relatively firm primitive streak.
Steps of folding: (Figures 5.6 & 7)
spans.label: Steps of folding

spans.text: • Expansion of the amniotic cavity leads to ventral shift of the amnio-ectodermal
junction towards the endoderm with subsequent dorsal bulge of the embryo
inside the amniotic cavity.
• Cranio-caudal elongation of the embryonic disc due to growth of neural tube and
somites leads to formation of head and tail folds.
• Lateral folds when completed, they make the embryo acquire a cylindrical shape
with the following arrangement of the three layers of the embryonic disc (from
outer to inner): ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm.
(Anatomy) Embryonic Period 27
Results of folding: (Figures 5. 8 – 10)
spans.label: Results of folding

spans.text: 1. Embryonic disc is transformed into cylindrical shape that has a body cavity.
2. Amniotic cavity surrounds the embryo.
3. Formation of the primitive umbilical ring: It is the defect in the ventral abdominal
wall at which the lateral folds fail to fuse due to the presence of connecting stalk,
allantois and vitelline duct.
4. Formation of the mucosa of the gut from the endoderm. The gut is divided into
foregut in the head fold, hindgut in the tail fold and midgut in the middle between
the lateral folds.
5. Secondary (definitive) yolk sac is compressed from all directions to form vitelline
duct that is connected to midgut by vitelline (vitello-intestinal) duct.
6. Formation of the forebrain bulge that is formed in head of the embryo due to
growing forebrain.
7. Formation of the pericardial bulge that is formed due to growing heart and
pericardium.
8. Formation of the stomodeum that is an ectodermal depression between
forebrain and pericardial bulges. It is separated from the foregut by bucco-
pharyngeal membrane.
9. Formation of ventral and dorsal mesenteries as after folding, the two peritoneal
canal approaches the gut and meat each other on ventral and dorsal aspects of
the gut to form the mesenteries.
10. Reversal of position:
a) In the head fold, septum transverse becomes caudal instead of being the
most cranial before folding. Bucco-pharyngeal membrane becomes the
most cranial structure after folding.
b) In the tail fold, connecting stalk with allantois becomes more cranial and
ventral instead of being the most caudal before folding. Cloacal
membrane becomes the most caudal after folding.

They are the tissues that play an important role in protection, support and provide the
embryo with nutrition. They are:

Placenta
The placenta is a remarkable, temporary organ that develops in the uterus during
pregnancy. It serves as the vital connection and communication interface between the
mother and the developing fetus.
External features of full-term placenta (Figure 6.1)
Shape: Disc-shaped.
spans.label: Shape

spans.text: Thickness: 3 cm.
spans.label: Thickness

spans.text: Site: Mostly in the upper segment of the posterior wall of the uterine cavity near
spans.label: Site

spans.text: Surfaces: It has two surfaces:
spans.label: Surfaces

spans.text: Fetal surface: It is the surface of placenta that faces the fetus. It is smooth and covered
spans.label: Fetal surface

spans.text: with transparent amnion. Umbilical cord is attached near the center of this surface.
Fetal surface shows the umbilical vessels that leaves umbilical cord and run on this
surface to reach the tertiary villi.
(Anatomy) Fetal Membranes 30
Maternal surface: It is the surface of placenta that is fixed to the wall of uterus. It shows
spans.label: Maternal surface

spans.text: the presence of 15 – 20 elevations that are called cotyledons that are separated from
each other by grooves. It is covered by a thin layer of decidua basalis.
Formation of placenta:
Placenta is formed by a union between two main plates:
I-Maternal part: It is the decidual plate (decidua basalis).
spans.label: I-Maternal part

spans.text: II-Fetal part: It is the chorionic plate (chorion frondosum).
spans.label: II-Fetal part

spans.text: Structure of placenta (Figure 6.2)
Placenta is composed of:
1-Chorionic plate: It is formed of the following structures (from external of placenta to its
internal):
1. Amnion.
2. Somatopleuric (somatic) extra-embryonic mesoderm.
3. Cytotrophoblast.
4. Syncytiotrophoblast.
Chorionic plate shows the presence of umbilical vessels in their way to enter villi
(arteries) and leaving villi (veins).
2-Decidual plate: It is formed of (from external of placenta to its internal):
1. Decidua basalis that contains maternal arterioles and venules as well as
uterine glands.
2. Cytotrophoblastic shell.
3. Syncytiotrophoblast that lines the intervillous spaces.
3-Tertiary villi: They are villi of chorion frondosum (chorionic plate) and each villus is
composed of (from outer layer of the villus to its core):
1. Syncytiotrophoblast.
2. Cytotrophoblast.
3. Somatic (somatopleuric) mesoderm.
4. Endothelium of fetal blood vessels.
Each tertiary villus is composed of the following parts:
1- Stem (anchoring) part: It is the median part of the villus that extends from the
chorion to decidua basalis.
(Anatomy) Fetal Membranes 31
2- Absorbing (free or floating) parts: They are side branches from the main stem part
of the villus. They are free branches that float in maternal blood inside the
intervillous spaces.
Intervillous spaces:
They are intercommunicating spaces that are present between tertiary villi and receive
floating branches of tertiary villi. They contain maternal blood that is derived from
uterine arterioles of the decidua basalis. They contain 150 ml blood that is changed 3 –
4 times / min.
Placental (decidual) septa:
They are incomplete septa that extends from decidual plate to the cavity of intervillous
spaces. They appear during the 4th and 5th gestational months. Each septum is
composed of a core of decidua basalis that is covered with cytotrophoblast and
syncytiotrophoblast. Opposite each septum, there is a groove on the maternal surface.
These grooves separate between the cotyledons.
Placental circulation: (Figure 6.3)
spans.label: Placental circulation

spans.text: It is the circulation of blood inside the placenta and composed of:
I-Maternal part:
Arterial blood flows to the intervillous spaces through 80 -100 decidual arterioles. Full
term placenta contains about 150 ml of maternal blood that is changed 3 – 4 times /
min. After the exchange of material between maternal and fetal blood, blood of
intervillous spaces flows back towards the decidual venules.
II-Fetal part:
Umbilical arteries carry fetal blood from the fetus to placenta through the umbilical cord.
They run on the fetal surface of the placenta to enter the tertiary villi. After the
exchange of material with maternal blood, fetal blood is drained through an umbilical
vein back to the fetus.
(Anatomy) Fetal Membranes 32
Placental barrier (membrane) (Figure 6.4)
It is a membrane that separates maternal blood inside the intervillous spaces from fetal
blood inside tertiary villi.
Structure of placental barrier:
A- During early pregnancy, it is composed of (from maternal to fetal side)
syncytiotrophoblast, cytotrophoblast, somatic mesoderm and endothelium of
fetal blood vessels.
B- During the second half of pregnancy (from the 4th month) it is composed of
syncytiotrophoblast and endothelium of fetal blood vessels. So, the placental
barrier becomes thinner to allow rapid exchange of nutrients and gases giving
adequate nutrition to the larger fetus.
Functions of placental barrier:
 It separates between the fetal and maternal blood.
 It permits the exchange of nutrients, gases and waste products between
maternal and fetal blood.
 It prevents the passage of bacteria and most viruses except HIV, poliomyelitis,
rubella, cytomegalovirus and measles.
 It mostly prevents the passage of toxic material and maternal hormones.
(Anatomy) Fetal Membranes 33
Functions of placenta
1-Exchange of metabolic products, as it allows transmission of nutritive substances
from maternal to fetal blood and waste products in the opposite direction.
2-Exchange of gases: transmission of oxygen to fetal blood and CO2 from fetal to
maternal blood.
3-Transmission of maternal antibodies to the fetal blood starting from the 14th week, so
the fetus will gain immunity.
4-Placenta has an endocrine function as it produces:
 Progesterone hormone that maintains the endometrium of pregnancy.
 Estrogen hormone stimulates uterine growth and maturation of mammary gland.
 Human chorionic gonadotropins (HCG) maintain the corpus luteum till the 4th
month. It is used to detect pregnancy.
 Somatomammotropin gives the fetus priority on maternal blood glucose. It also
promotes breast development.
5-Placenta has a protective role as it prevents the passage of bacteria and most
viruses.
6-Placenta has an excretory function as it gets rid of fetal urea and creatinine.
Congenital anomalies of placenta: (Figures 6.5 – 7)
spans.label: Congenital anomalies of placenta

spans.text: 1-In position (placenta is in the lower segment of uterine cavity): see chapter 3
2-In shape: placenta may be bilobed or trilobed.
3-In number: It is either a twin placenta or accessory placenta with a single umbilical
cord that is attached to the main placenta.
4-In attachment of umbilical cord:
a) Velamentous placenta: The umbilical cord is attached to placenta through
amniotic membrane.
b) Battledore placenta: The umbilical cord is attached to the margin of the placenta.
5-In diameter: Thinner and wider placenta is called placenta membranacea.
6-In infiltration: Deep infiltration of placenta to the wall of the uterus.
 Placenta accreta: Placenta infiltrates till the myometrium.
 Placenta increta: Placenta infiltrates the myometrium.
 Placenta percreta: Placenta infiltrates till the covering peritoneum.

Formation of the amniotic cavity (Figure 6.8)
Amniotic cavity appears on the 8th day within the cells of the inner cell mass
(embryoblast). After formation of the amniotic cavity, the embryoblast cells differentiate
into amnioblast cells (adjacent to cytotrophoblast) and epiblast cells (adjacent to
hypoblast). Amnio-ectodermal junction is the meeting between amnion and periphery of
ectoderm.
Results of expansion of the amniotic cavity (Figures 6.8 & 9)
1. Folding of the embryonic disc with formation of primitive umbilical ring that is
surrounded with amnio-ectodermal junction.
2. Formation of sheath of amnion around the umbilical cord.
3. Amnion covers the fetal surface of placenta.
4. At the beginning of the third month, amnion comes in contact with chorion,
forming amniochrorionic membrane with obliteration of chorionic cavity.
5. At the end of the third month, amniochorionic membrane covered with decidua
capsularis comes in contact with decidua parietalis with obliteration of uterine

Amniotic fluid
It is clear watery fluid that is mainly composed of water, electrolytes, protein,
carbohydrates, lipids, phospholipids, and urea. It is firstly produced by amnioblast cells,
then it is derived from maternal blood by osmosis. After kidney development, fetal urine
is added to the amniotic fluid starting from the 5th month. Volume of the amniotic fluid
ranges between 1.0 – 1.5 liter from 37th week till birth. Recent studies show that
amniotic fluid contains considerable amounts of stem cells.
Functions of the amniotic fluid
A-At early pregnancy:
1. It acts as shock absorbent protecting the fetus from external trauma.
2. It acts as a thermal insulator to ensure constant fetal temperature.
3. It prevents the adhesion of the fetus to the wall of the uterus.
4. It prevents adhesion of the fetal body parts. e.g. limb to the body.
B-At late pregnancy:
1. It gives a space for fetal movements that are essential for the development of
fetal muscles.
2. It gives a space for accumulation of fetal urine.
3. At the beginning of the 5th month, the fetus starts to swallow the amniotic fluid to
learn how to suckle.
C-During delivery:
1. It protects the fetus against uterine contractions.
2. Fore bag of amniotic sac helps gradual dilatation of the cervical canal.
3. Rupture of the amniotic sac is the sign of the start of labor.
4. Sterile amniotic fluid washes vagina just before passage of the fetus during
delivery.
D-Stem cells:
 Amniotic fluid is a source of stem cells.
(Anatomy) Fetal Membranes 37
Abnormalities of the amniotic fluid volume
Polyhydramnios:
It is case of increased amniotic fluid to be more than two liters at full-term.
• Unknown cause in 35 % of cases.
• Maternal diabetes.
• Congenital malformation of esophagus e.g. esophageal atresia that interferes
with normal fetal swallowing.
• Congenital malformation of the central nervous system e.g. anencephaly.
Oligohydramnios:
It is the decrease of the amniotic fluid to be less than 400 ml at full term.
It may result from bilateral renal agenesis or obstruction of the urinary tract.
Premature rupture of amniotic sac
It is the commonest cause of preterm labor.

It is the cord that connects the fetus with placenta.
Morphology of the cord at full term (Figure 6.10)
Attachments: It extends between the fetal surface of the placenta and ventral aspect
spans.label: Attachments

spans.text: of the fetal abdominal wall.
Diameter: 2 cm
spans.label: Diameter

spans.text: Shape: It is tortuous due to wavy course of umbilical arteries; wider curve of an
spans.label: Shape

but with no fetal stress.
Structure: It contains two umbilical arteries and one umbilical vein that are embedded

Functions of the umbilical cord
1. It contains umbilical vessels that transmit fetal blood between the fetus and
placenta.
2. It allows free mobility of the fetus.
Development of the umbilical cord (Figure 6.11)
A-Formation of the primitive umbilical ring
During the 4th gestational week, expansion of amniotic cavity leads to folding of the
embryonic disc with ventral shift of the amnio-ectodermal junction that surrounds the
primitive umbilical ring.
Contents of the primitive umbilical ring
1. Allantois and umbilical vessels inside the connecting stalk.
2. Vitelline (vitello-intestinal) duct and vitelline vessels.
B-Formation of primitive umbilical cord
Amnion of expanded amniotic cavity ensheathes the structures that pass through the
primitive umbilical ring to form the primitive umbilical cord.
Contents of the primitive umbilical cord
1. Secondary (definitive) yolk sac, vitelline duct and vitelline vessels.
2. Connecting stalk, remnant of allantois and umbilical vessels.
3. On the 6th week, intestinal loops herniate in the proximal part of the primitive
cord (physiological umbilical hernia).
C-Formation of definitive umbilical cord
• Intestinal loop returns to the abdominal cavity by the 3rd month.
• Obliteration of one umbilical vein and extra-embryonic part of vitelline vessels.
• Degeneration of vitelline duct secondary yolk sac and extra-embryonic part of
allantois.
• Formation of Wharton’s jelly from the mesoderm of connecting stalk.
(Anatomy) Fetal Membranes 39
Congenital anomalies of the umbilical cord (Figure 6.12)
• Short cord: It leads to limitation of movements of the fetus and premature
separation of placenta during delivery.
• Long cord: It may encircle the neck of the fetus or may form a true knot. Both
are serious life-threatening conditions.
• Congenital umbilical hernia (omphalocele): The proximal part of the cord
contains loops of intestine due to failure of return of intestine to the abdominal
• Presence of one umbilical artery due to degeneration of the other artery.
• Abnormal attachment of umbilical cord to placenta; either to the margin of
placenta (battledore placenta) or it may end outside the placenta where the
umbilical vessels run through the amnion to reach the fetal surface of placenta.
Yolk Sac
It is one of fetal membranes that has an important role in supporting the human
Development of the yolk sac (Figures 6.13 & 14)
1-Primary yolk sac:
It is formed at the 9th gestational day, when flat cells derived from hypoblast form
Heuser’s membrane that lines the blastocele (cavity of the blastocyst).
2-Secondary (definitive) yolk sac:
It is formed on the 13th gestational day due to the following changes:
• New cells that are derived from hypoblast and form a new lining to Heuser’s
membrane.
• Reduction of the size of yolk sac due to pinching off a part by growing chorionic
• Formation of allantois: It is a diverticulum which extends from the caudal wall of
secondary yolk sac to the connecting stalk.
3-After folding
Secondary (definitive) yolk sac becomes compressed to form a vitelline (vitello-
intestinal) duct that connects midgut with the part of yolk sac that remains outside the
folded embryonic disc.
(Anatomy) Fetal Membranes 40
Fate of yolk sac
Secondary (definitive) yolk sac and vitelline duct (in primitive umbilical cord) are
gradually reduced in size and finally degenerate.
Functions of yolk sac
 Formation of gut: With endoderm, yolk sac shares in the formation of gut.
 Formation of apex of urinary bladder: From the proximal part of allantois.
 Development of primordial germ cells: At the 2nd week, epiblast migrate to the
wall of the caudal part of the yolk sac to form primordial germ cells.
 Formation of blood vessels of the gut: They develop in the mesoderm around
vitelline duct. Intra-embryonic part of vitelline vessels forms blood supply of gut
while the extra-embryonic part disappears.
 Formation of blood cells: that are developed in the splanchnic extra-embryonic
mesoderm of yolk sac in early pregnancy.

It is a collection of connective tissue under the skin. It covers the body wall
and limbs. It includes: superficial, deep and internal fasciae.
A) Superficial Fascia
Structure:
 It is a layer of loose CT lies just
deep to the skin and allows the
skin to move more or less freely over the
underlying structures.
 It contains a variable quantity of fat, more in
females:
o Fat is abundant in gluteal region, anterior abdominal wall and breast.
o Fat is less in the limbs and absent in the eyelid, penis and scrotum.
(Anatomy) Fascia 47
Functions:
1) Prevents the heat loss from the body, so
it acts as thermal insulator.
2) Softens and smoothens the surface of
the body.
3) Facilitates the movement of the skin
over the underlying structures.
4) Medium to conduct the nerves, vessels
and lymphatics to the skin.
5) Contains skin muscles, as in face (muscles of expression).
6) Contains special types of glands as mammary glands.
B) Deep Fascia
Structure: It is non elastic membrane formed of compact and regular collagen
spans.label: Structure

spans.text: fibers. It is well defined in the limbs and very strong and thick in palm and sole. It is
absent in the face and in the anterior wall of abdomen.
Parts and Functions:
1- Formation of broad sheets: around groups of body muscles to give muscle
attachment, fix underlying structures in position and help the venous return.
2- Formation of intermuscular septa and interosseous membranes: They
separate different muscle groups having different actions and nerve supply. They
also increase the surface area for muscle attachment.
3- Formation of retinacula: They are localized transverse thickened bands around
wrist and ankle joints to keep the tendons in position.
4- Formation of palmar aponeurosis (in the palm) and plantar aponeurosis (in
the sole): They are very thick and strong layers of the deep fascia to protect the
underlying vessels, nerves and tendons.
5- Formation of fibrous sheaths around big vessels e.g. Carotid sheath in the
neck around common carotid artery, internal jugular vein and vagus.

Skeletal System
It is a hard type of connective tissue which forms the skeleton.
 Functions of Skeleton:
a. Gives the specific shape to the body.
b. Provides the central axis of the body. Also the skeleton of both upper and
lower limbs.
c. Protects the vital organs: the skull protects the brain, and thoracic cage
protects the heart and lungs.
d. Provides surface area for muscular attachment.
e. Transmits and supports the body weight e.g. vertebral column transmits
the weight of the head and trunk to the bony pelvis then through the bones of
lower limbs to the feet and lastly to the ground.
f. Forms the joints to make an important part of the locomotor system.
g. Forms the blood elements in the bone marrow.
h. Stores calcium salts.

 Types (Varieties) of the Synovial Joints
A- According to the number of articulating bones:
1. Simple joints: Between two bones e.g. shoulder.
2. Compound joints: Between more than two bones e.g. elbow.
3. Complex joints: Contain intra-articular structures e.g. knee joint.
B- According to the axis of movement and the shape of the articular
surfaces:
I. Uni-axial joints
In this type of joints the movements take place around a single axis.
According to the direction of axis there are 2 types:
a- One transverse axis: e.g. elbow joint (hinge joint).
b- One longitudinal axis: e.g. superior radio ulnar joint (pivot joint).
According to the shape of the articular surfaces there are 2 types:
1- Hinge joint: The convex articular surface is trochlea-like. The joint is uni-axial
with one transverse axis. The movement is flexion and extension only due to
strong collateral ligaments, e.g. elbow.
2- Pivot joint: articulating surface consist of a central bony pivot (axis)
surrounded by a fibro-osseous ring, e.g. superior radio-ulnar joint. The
movement of this joint is rotation around a longitudinal axis .

II. Bi-axial joints
The movements take place around 2 axes perpendicular to each other.
According to the shape of the articular surfaces there are 3 types:
1- Condylar joint:
It consists of either 2 separate convex surfaces (condyles) which articulate with 2
concave surfaces, e.g. knee joint (bicondylar) or one condyle articulating with one
concave surface e.g. temporomandibular joint (TMJ) (unicondylar).
2- Ellipsoid joint:
It is formed by the articulation of an oval convex surface (carpal bones) with an
elliptical concave surface (inferior surface of radius and the articular disc of ulna)
e.g. wrist joint.
3- Saddle joint:
The articulating surfaces of this joint are concavo-convex e.g. carpometacarpal
joint of thumb.
(Anatomy) Articular system 64

 In this type of joints, the movements occurs around 3 axes.
 The articular surface consists of a globular rounded bone articulates with
a concave socket. They are the most freely mobile joints in the body.
 According to the shape of the articular surfaces, they are called ball and socket
joints, e.g. shoulder and hip joints.

Types of the Muscle Action
A purposeful movement is not done by the action of one muscle but by a group of
muscles which should act together.
According to the role of the muscle, there are 4 types of muscle actions:
1- Prime mover:
The muscle which initiates and maintains a movement; also called agonist.
2- Antagonist:
The muscle which opposes the action of the prime mover.
3- Fixator (Stabilizer):
The muscles which fix the origin of the prime mover or stabilize the joint upon
which the muscle acts.
4- Synergist:
Sometimes the prime mover muscle crosses many joints before it reaches its
insertion. Synergistic muscles will contract to eliminate the unwanted movements
at the crossed joints. Therefore the action of the prime mover on the desired joint
becomes maximal.

A- Systemic circulation:
 Oxygenated blood in the left ventricle passes through the aorta and its branches
to reach all the tissues of the body, where exchange of gases and materials
 Deoxygenated blood is collected by small veins, then by large veins and finally
by superior and inferior venae cava into the right atrium.

circulation ends and a new cycle starts.
B- Pulmonary circulation:

Lymphatic system
 This is a system which is responsible for the circulation of the lymph (clear
colorless fluid, rich in protein) from the tissue spaces (intercellular spaces) to the
blood stream.
 Lymphatic system consists of 3 parts:
(a) Lymph vessels.
(b) Lymphoid tissues as lymph nodes, spleen, tonsils and thymus.
(c) Free cells (lymphocytes): including B- and t- lymphocytes.
Lymph Vessels
 They are fine vessels present in the tissue spaces uniting together to form larger
lymph vessels which join the lymph nodes.
 There are 2 types of lymph vessels:
1) Afferent lymph vessels: They open into the periphery of the lymph nodes at their
convex borders and carry lymph to them.
2) Efferent lymph vessels: They emerge from the hilum of the lymph nodes and
carry the lymph away from them. All lymph vessels in the body are collected into 2
large lymph ducts in the root of the neck including:
A) Thoracic duct drains the left side of head, neck and left upper limb, left half of
thorax and whole body below diaphragm.
(Anatomy) Lymphatic system 83
B) Right lymphatic duct drains the right side of
head and neck, right half of thorax and right
upper limb.
The two ducts open into two large veins
present at the root of the neck.
Characters of the lymph vessels:
1. They begin blindly in the tissue spaces.
2. Walls contain wide pores which allow the
passage of fat and proteins.
3. They have many valves which make the flow
of lymph in one direction.
4. Lymph vessels are absent in brain and spinal
cord (CNS), bone marrow and avascular
structures e.g. cartilage, cornea and hair.
Factors which help the flow and the movement of lymph:
1) Arterial pulsations.
2) Muscular contractions.
3) Intra thoracic negative pressure
4) Peristaltic movement of the intestine.

 Shape: lymph nodes are oval or
kidney-shaped small bodies.
 Site: along the course of lymph
vessels in groups in fixed sites:
a. At the limb roots: axillary (in

b. In the neck, on both its sides and at its junction with the head.

foreign bodies.

Deep Fascia of the Forearm
(Antebrachial Fascia)
The deep fascia of the forearm is called antebrachial fascia and it is thicker on the
posterior than on the anterior surface of the forearm. It gives partial origin to the
muscles of the forearm both in front and behind.
- Sites of thickening of the antebrachial fascia:
1. It is strengthened above by the bicipital aponeurosis.
2. Along the posterior border of the ulna, the deep fascia forms a strong ulnar
aponeurosis which gives origin to the following muscles:
a. Flexor carpi ulnaris
b. Extensor carpi ulnaris
c. Flexor digitorum profundus
3. The deep fascia is thickened in the region of the wrist, where it forms two
bands, one in front called flexor retinaculum and one behind called
extensor retinaculum.

DEEP FASCIA OF THE PALM
It consists of 3 parts (Fig.80):
 Lateral part: thin and covers the thenar eminence.
 Medial part: thin and covers the hypothenar eminence.
 Central part: thick and strong and covers the intermediate compartment. It is
called the palmar aponeurosis.
Palmar Aponeurosis
It forms the central part of the deep fascia of the palm. It is the thickest and strongest
part of it. It is firmly attached to the overlying skin of the palm by dense fibrous tissue.
- Functions: it protects the tendons, vessels and nerves which go to the fingers.

becomes continuous with the fibrous flexor sheath of one of the medial four

 Lateral margin: it is continuous with the deep fascia covering the thenar
eminence which is much thinner.

Superficial Distal Pulp Space of the Finger
 It is the pulp space of the distal phalanx (at the tip of the finger) (Fig. 83).
 It is very tightly packed with small lobules of subcutaneous fat separated by many
fibrous septa, which pass from the skin to the periosteum of the distal phalanx.
When it is inflamed, it is very painful because pus will be entrapped under tension
in this narrow space and compresses on the nerves.
Blood vessels of the shaft and head, but not of the base, of the terminal
phalanx traverse the pulp space.
Severe infection of the pulp space may result in thrombosis of the vessels of
the shaft and head of the distal phalanx and their consequent death. The base
is spared (not affected).

A. Common Flexor Sheath (Ulnar Bursa):
 Encloses 8 tendons (Flexor Digitorum Superficialis & Profundus) as they pass

finger’s sheath.
B. Flexor Pollicis Sheath (Radial Bursa):
 Encloses the Flexor Pollicis Longus tendon.

 Enclose flexor tendons in each finger.
 Two layers: one on the tendon, one lining the canal.
 Extend proximally to the distal palm crease (except the little finger, which
connects with the ulnar bursa), and
distally to the tendon insertions

They are the two terminal branches of ulnar nerve, superficial and deep branches,

spans.label: Course and relations

- Branches:
1. Superficial branch:
 Arises in front of the flexor retinaculum.
 It descends deep to the palmaris brevis muscle, supplying it and then
divides into two palmar digital branches to supply the skin on the palmar
surfaces of little finger and medial half of the ring finger (the medial 11/2

deep branch of the ulnar artery.

hamate and turns laterally across the palm, lying in the concavity of the deep
palmar arch (deep to the flexor tendons).
 It ends near the lateral border of the palm by breaking up into terminal
branches.
 It gives the following branches:

The veins of the upper limb are divided into
superficial and deep groups, which

A- superficial dorsal venous network or arch:
It is a network of veins in the superficial fascia on the dorsum of hand. It
receives the dorsal digital and the metacarpal veins.
B- Cephalic Vein:
- It begins from the lateral end of the dorsal venous arch just behind the styloid
process of radius.
- It runs upwards to reach the anterior surface of the forearm, where it ascends
in its lateral side.
- Then, it crosses the lateral part of the roof of cubital fossa to reach the arm.
- In the arm, it runs in a groove along its lateral side.
- Finally, it reaches the delto-pectoral groove.

Ulnar Nerve Injury
- Causes:
 Posterior to the medial epicondyle of the humerus: fracture, dislocation or
compression of the elbow joint.
 In the cubital tunnel formed by the tendinous arch connecting the humeral and
ulnar heads of the flexor carpi ulnaris: compression
 At the wrist: Cut or stab
- Results:
1. Motor effect:
A. Effect of injury at
the wrist:
 Partial claw hand:
Extension of metacarpo-phalangeal joints of the 4th and 5th fingers
and flexion of their interphalangeal joints due to paralysis of their
lumbricals and interossei. The corresponding joints of the 2nd and
3rd fingers are less affected because their lumbricals are intact as
they are supplied by the median nerve.
 Loss of abduction and adduction of the fingers due to paralysis
of the interossei. The patient is unable to grip a piece of paper
placed between the fingers.
 Loss of adduction of the thumb due to paralysis of the adductor
pollicis. The patient is unable to grip a piece of paper placed
between the thumb and index.
 Flattening of the hypothenar eminence due to wasting of the
hypothenar muscles and hollowing between the metacarpal bones
on the dorsum of the hand due to paralysis of the interossei.

B. Effect of injury above or at the elbow:
 Clawing of the hand becomes less apparent in the 4th and 5th
fingers due to paralysis of the medial half of the flexor digitorum
profundus.
 Radial deviation of the hand due to paralysis of the flexor carpi
ulnaris.
 Loss of abduction and adduction of the fingers.
 Loss of adduction of the thumb.
 Flattening of the hypothenar eminence and hollowing between the
metacarpal bones on the dorsum of the hand.
2. Sensory effect:
A. Effect of injury at the wrist:
The ulnar nerve and its palmar cutaneous branch are usually affected
leading to loss of sensation over the medial 1/3 of the palm and the
palmer surface of the medial 1 1/2 fingers.
B. Effect of injury above or at the elbow:
Loss of sensation over the medial 1/3 of the palm, the medial 1 1/2
fingers both anteriorly and posteriorly and the medial 1/3 of the back of
the hand.

 Pronator syndrome: it is a nerve entrapment syndrome caused by

- Cause:

while passing in the spiral groove.

JOINTS OF THE UPPER LIMB
Joints of Shoulder Girdle
1. Acromio-Clavicular Joint:
- Type: synovial, plane variety.
spans.label: Type

spans.text: - Bony parts (articular surfaces):
 Acromial end of clavicle.
 Medial margin of acromion.
- Articular disc: the joint usually contains an articular disc, which divides its
spans.label: Articular disc

spans.text: cavity into 2 incomplete compartments (medial and lateral).
- Capsule: it surrounds the joint and is strengthened above by acromio-clavicular
spans.label: Capsule

spans.text: ligament.
- Functions:
 It shares a little in the movements of shoulder girdle.
 It shares in transmitting forces from the upper limb to the clavicle; but the
main medium transmitting forces from the upper limb to clavicle is the
coraco-clavicular ligament.
* Coraco-clavicular ligament
It is very strong bond connecting the clavicle with the coracoid process of the
scapula.
- Parts: it consists of two incompletely separated parts:
spans.label: Parts

spans.text: A. Trapezoid part
 Forms the anterolateral part of the coraco-clavicular ligament.
 Quadrilateral in shape; its posterior border is joined with the conoid
 (Anatomy) Joints of Upper Limb 
 Attached below to the upper surface of the coracoid process and
above to the trapezoid line on the lower surface of the lateral third of
the clavicle.
B. Conoid part
 Forms the posteromedial part of the coraco-clavicular ligament.
 A dense band of fibrous tissue.
 Attached below to the upper and posterior aspect of the bend of the
coracoid process of scapula and above to the conoid tubercle of
clavicle.
- Function:
 It limits the movements of acromio-clavicular joint and prevents
dislocation of the acromial end of the clavicle.
 It is the main medium by which the scapula and the upper limb are
suspended from the clavicle. If the clavicle is fractured medial to the
attachment of coraco-clavicular ligament, the upper limb drops.
Fig. 117: Anterior view of acromioclavicular joint
 (Anatomy) Joints of Upper Limb 
2. Sterno-clavicular Joint:
- Type: Synovial; modified saddle joint.
spans.label: Type

spans.text: - Bony parts (articular surfaces):
Clavicular notch of manubrium sterni and first costal cartilage.
Sternal (medial) end of the clavicle.
- Intra-articular disc:
 It is a flat circular disc of fibro- cartilage interposed between the articulating
surfaces and is attached by its
circumference to the fibrous
capsule.
 It divides the joint cavity into two
separate cavities.
 Functions:
It absorbs the forces transmitted to the
joint from the shoulder region through Fig. 118: sternoclavicular joint
the clavicle& prevents dislocation of the sternal end of the clavicle.
- Capsule:
Surrounds the joint completely. It is thicker in front and behind; but is thin
above and below.
- Ligaments:
1. Anterior sterno-clavicular ligament: covers the anterior surface of the joint.
2. Posterior sterno-clavicular ligament: covers the posterior surface of the
3. Interclavicular ligament:
It passes from the upper aspect of the sternal end of one clavicle to that of
the other, crossing above the upper margin of manubrium sterni and is
attached to it.
4. Costo-clavicular ligament:
 It is attached below to the upper aspect of 1st costo-chondral junction and
above to the margins of the impression of the lower surface of medial end of
the clavicle. It prevents excessive elevation and protraction of the clavicle
(the same function of subclavius muscle, which acts as a dynamic
ligament).
- Stability: it is a stable joint. Its strength depends on its ligaments and the intra-
spans.label: Stability

spans.text: articular disc.
Fig. 119: ligaments of
sternoclavicular joint

* Movements of the shoulder girdle:
Movements of the shoulder girdle occur at both acromioclavicular and
sternoclavicular joints. The scapula is the main element of the girdle, which
moves on the clavicle at the acromioclavicular joint, but the movement at this
joint is limited. However, the movement at the sternoclavicular joint increases
the range of movement of the scapula.
A. Elevation
1. Upper fibers of trapezius 2. Levator scapulae
3. Rhomboid major and minor
B. Depression
1. Pectoralis minor 2. Inferior fibers of trapezius
C. Rotation up (glenoid cavity faces upwards):
1. Upper and lower fibers of trapezius 2. Serratus anterior
D. Rotation down (glenoid cavity faces downward):
1. Levator scapulae 2. Rhomboideus major
3. Rhomboideus minor
E. Protraction (pulling forwards):
1. Serratus anterior
2. Pectoralis minor
F. Retraction (pulling backwards
towards the vertebrae):
1. Middle fibers of trapezius
2. Rhomboideus major
3. Rhomboideus minor
